extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecution practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements amount to "significantly more" than a judicial exception under Alice/Mayo Step 2B; instructs examiners how to treat well-understood/routine/conventional elements, meaningful limitations, and mere instructions to apply an exception. Includes field-specific examples and case law references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity consideration (MPEP §2106.05(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a determination whether the additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General guidance: this consideration overlaps with other Step 2B considerations (improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity) and examiners should analyze all relevant considerations together. Key points: (1) An additional element known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine; novelty/obviousness inquiries are separate from eligibility (e.g., Enfish). (2) A prior art search is not necessary to determine whether an element is well-understood, routine, conventional; examiners may rely on what courts or those in the art recognize and on the examiner's own expertise — only conclude an element is conventional if it can be readily concluded that it is widely prevalent or in common use. (3) Even if individual elements are conventional, their combination may be an inventive concept (e.g., Diamond v. Diehr; Rapid Litigation Mgmt.; BASCOM). The specification may indicate elements are well-known or conventional; courts may take judicial notice. A rejection under Step 2B should only be made if the examiner, based on expertise, can readily conclude the additional elements do not amount to significantly more. See also MPEP §2106.07(a). Examples of elements courts have recognized as well-understood/routine/conventional when recited generically: computer functions (receiving/transmitting data over a network; repetitive calculations; electronic recordkeeping; storing/retrieving in memory; OCR; browser navigation), life-science laboratory techniques (measuring biomarkers, PCR, detecting DNA/enzymes, immunization, DNA analysis/sequencing, freezing/thawing cells, hybridizing probes), and other activities (recording a customer order; shuffling/dealing cards; restricting access by requiring viewing an advertisement; identifying undeliverable mail; presenting offers and gathering statistics; determining estimated outcome and setting a price; arranging/sorting information). Caveat: listing examples does not mean all computer functions are conventional; generic computer components used only to implement an abstract idea may render a claim ineligible, but generic components in combination can sometimes perform non-generic functions (e.g., DDR Holdings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations (MPEP §2106.05(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim directed to a judicial exception to be patent-eligible, it must include additional features that ensure the claim applies the exception in a meaningful way (i.e., more than drafting to monopolize the exception); such additional features are "meaningful limitations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The considerations in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(d) (e.g., improvement, particular machine, particular transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional) are examples of meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr—additional physical steps applying a mathematical equation were meaningful because they limited the equation to a practical application; Classen—analysis plus an immunization step integrated results into a specific, tangible application; contrast Alice and OIP Technologies—recitation of a generic computer or routine data-gathering steps did not meaningfully limit the abstract idea. When evaluating meaningful limitations, consider additional elements both individually and in combination; combinations of otherwise-generic elements can amount to significantly more (Diamond, BASCOM). Examiners should, when appropriate, explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (MPEP §2106.05(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim element (or combination) that merely recites the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) or is nothing more than an instruction to implement an abstract idea/other exception (for example, on a generic computer) does not amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit authority (Mayo, Alice, Benson) show that merely adding a generic computer or generic implementation is insufficient. Examiners should avoid treating drafting choices as dispositive; instead analyze whether the additional elements do more than state the exception and add 'apply it.' Requiring more than mere instructions does not require narrow claims—some broad claims are eligible and some narrow claims are ineligible—so evaluate each claim on its merits and alongside other Step 2B considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional). For claim limitations that appear to be mere instructions to apply an exception, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection. Considerations examiners may use include: (1) Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., fails to recite details or mechanism for accomplishing the result). Result-oriented or functional claim language that effectively covers any solution is equivalent to 'apply it' (see Electric Power; Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One). Other cited cases illustrate where claimed steps were found to be mere instructions (Mayo, Alice, Benson) or where recitations merely linked the idea to a technological environment without meaningful limitation.
